# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review of Technique, Clinical Outcomes, and Future Directions

## Introduction
Vascular access is a fundamental determinant of success in structural heart disease (SHD) interventions. Although transfemoral (TF) retrograde arterial access remains the preferred clinical approach for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and other large-bore procedures, approximately 10% to 15% of candidates present with hostile iliofemoral anatomy, severe calcification, tortuosity, or concomitant aneurysmal disease that precludes safe TF access [1]. Traditional surgical alternatives, such as transapical or direct transaortic access, carry significant surgical morbidity. Alternative percutaneous pathways, such as transsubclavian/transaxillary or transcarotid approaches, have emerged but are still restricted by vessel caliber, calcification, and risks of cerebrovascular events [2]. These challenges prompted the development of the fully percutaneous transcaval (or caval-aortic) access route [1]. Initially described in 2014, transcaval access involves establishing a temporary electrosurgical channel from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent abdominal aorta, permitting the retrograde delivery of large-bore sheaths and devices [1, 2].

## Procedural Principles and Technique
The mechanical feasibility of transcaval access relies on a unique physiological concept. Although deliberately creating an aortocaval fistula might seem counterintuitive, the surrounding retroperitoneal tissue pressure exceeds the central venous pressure within the IVC [2]. Consequently, any blood extravasating from the high-pressure abdominal aorta is directed back into the low-pressure venous channel, mitigating the risk of catastrophic retroperitoneal hemorrhage [2, 3].

Executing this procedure safely requires meticulous preprocedural planning. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) angiography is mandatory to identify a calcium-free "target window" on the abdominal aorta directly opposite a patent, non-calcified portion of the IVC, typically situated at the level of the third or fourth lumbar vertebrae (L3–L4) [4, 5]. During the procedure, a target snare is positioned in the abdominal aorta from an accessory arterial site, and a guiding catheter is advanced through the femoral vein to the pre-selected caval crossing site. A 0.014-inch guidewire is electrified using short bursts of radiofrequency energy (electrosurgical cautery) to traverse the caval-aortic barrier, and it is subsequently captured by the aortic snare [5, 6]. 

Following wire capture, a rigid guidewire is advanced across the tract, facilitating progressive tract dilation and the insertion of a large-bore delivery sheath. After the structural intervention is completed, the transcaval tract is closed percutaneously, typically using a nitinol-based cardiac occluder (such as a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus occluder) [3, 7]. Alternative electrosurgical crossing methods, such as laser-assisted access, have also been described [8]. While off-label use of structural heart occluders remains common, a dedicated transcaval closure device has undergone successful first-in-human evaluation [9].

## Outcomes and Comparisons in TAVR
The landmark National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) prospective trial confirmed the safety and efficacy of transcaval TAVR, reporting a 99% access success rate and excellent 12-month closure durability with minimal major vascular complications [3, 7]. Recent propensity-matched analyses comparing transcaval with transaxillary TAVR in contemporary practice have demonstrated lower stroke rates with the transcaval approach, likely because it completely avoids the manipulation of arch vessels [10]. Transcaval access also has comparable vascular and bleeding profiles to other alternative access methods but avoids the morbidity of thoracic incisions associated with surgical alternative accesses [11-13]. 

Meta-analyses of contemporary cohorts have substantiated these findings, showing high procedural success rates (>95%) and a steady decrease in vascular complications over time, reflecting an important operator learning curve and technical refinement [14, 15]. The real-world applicability of transcaval TAVR has also been validated in programs without prior transcaval experience, indicating that with structured proctoring, high procedural success and low complications are reproducible [16]. Furthermore, innovative clinical modifications, such as the use of transradial secondary access instead of transfemoral secondary access, further simplify the procedure and minimize vascular complications at accessory puncture sites [17]. When comparing options, transcaval and transcarotid (transcervical) approaches are generally preferred over thoracic options to "stay clear of the chest" [13, 18].

## Expanding Horizons Beyond TAVR
Although TAVR remains the primary indication for transcaval access, this strategy has been increasingly adopted for other large-bore interventions. It has emerged as a crucial alternative for percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (MCS) placement in cardiogenic shock [19]. In particular, transcaval delivery of the Impella 5.0 or 5.5 microaxial flow pumps allows for complete percutaneous placement of high-output left ventricular support in patients with prohibitive peripheral vascular disease, avoiding surgical axillary conduits [19-21]. Furthermore, modified transcaval techniques have facilitated venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) cannulation, such as left atrial venoarterial (LAVA)-ECMO, to provide simultaneous hemodynamic support and ventricular venting [22].

In vascular surgery, transcaval access has successfully enabled percutaneous thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [23]. It has also become a valuable route for the embolization of persistent type II endoleaks after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). Transcaval embolization of the aneurysm sac allows direct access to collateral vessel nidi, showing high technical success and clinical resolution rates in systematic reviews and clinical studies [24-26].

Finally, the versatility of the transcaval technique is highlighted by its feasibility in complex anatomies and previous reconstructions. Successful interventions have been performed across synthetic polyester aortic grafts [27], via sheathless approaches [28], through thrombosed infrarenal aneurysms [29], and in patients with congenital anomalies such as duplicated inferior vena cava [30].

## Conclusion
Transcaval access is a safe, percutaneous alternative for structural heart and vascular interventions requiring large-bore delivery when transfemoral access is unavailable. By avoiding thoracic surgery and manipulation of cerebral vessels, it significantly expands the pool of candidates for TAVR, mechanical circulatory support, and endovascular repair. Continued refinement of dedicated crossing and closure devices will likely facilitate more widespread adoption of this versatile technique.
